chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Washa, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Do not pick (fruits) at night, nor harvest at night, nor slaughter (the sacrificial animal) at night, nor sow at night, for if you do so, the contented one and the beggar will not come to you.

So I said, 'What is the contented one and the beggar?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The contented one is the one who is content with what you give him, and the beggar is the one who passes by you and asks you.'
And if you harvest at night, the beggar will not come asking.
And give its due on the day of its harvest.

At the time of harvest, meaning the grasping (taking) after the grasping when you harvest it; and when it comes out, the handful after the handful; and similarly at the time of picking (fruits), and similarly at the time of sowing.
And do not sow at night, because you give from the seed just as you give from the harvest.

key_terms.الْحَفْنَةَ: Handful (referring to taking portions of the harvest)
key_terms.الْقَانِعُ: The contented one (one who is satisfied with what is given without demanding more)
key_terms.الْقَبْضَةَ: Grasping/Taking (referring to the act of collecting the harvest)
key_terms.وَالْمُعْتَرُّ: The beggar (one who passes by and asks for charity)

ai.seo_question: Why should Muslims avoid harvesting or sowing at night according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links agricultural timing to social welfare, explaining that night work prevents the 'Qani' (contented recipient) and 'Mu'tarr' (beggar) from accessing charity, thereby missing the divine reward of 'Haqqahu' (its due). This practice reflects the Shia emphasis on integrating economic activity with communal responsibility, ensuring that the poor can actively seek sustenance during daylight hours when the harvest is fresh and visible.
